summary: The original Path Computation Element protocol let a PCE compute paths but did not let it track the state of existing label switched paths. This document adds extensions so a stateful PCE can synchronize LSP state with clients and, where allowed, take control of path parameters.

eli5.summary: A map app that only gives directions is helpful. One that also knows where every car currently is can do much better. This lets the path planner keep track of the routes in use.

subtitle: How a path computation server can learn about, and take control of, the label switched paths a router already runs.

tldr.problem: The original PCEP let a Path Computation Element (PCE) compute a path on request, but it gave the PCE no view of existing LSPs and no control over the timing and sequence of path computations.
tldr.mechanism: It adds a capability advertisement, two new messages (PCRpt and PCUpd), a state synchronization step and a per-LSP delegation mechanism, so the PCC reports LSP state and may hand control of chosen LSPs to the PCE.
tldr.outcome: A PCE can keep an up-to-date copy of a PCC's LSPs and, for LSPs delegated to it, decide when and how to change them, while the PCC keeps ownership of the LSP state. Later RFCs update this one.

today: RFC 8231 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8786, RFC 9353, RFC 9753, RFC 9756 and RFC 9862. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Stateful PCE
sections.content:
In PCEP as defined in RFC 5440, a Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute paths for MPLS Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (LSPs). The protocol makes no provision for the PCE to control the timing and sequence of path computations within and across PCEP sessions. RFC 8231 adds that, for MPLS-TE and GMPLS LSPs.

The RFC explains that in existing traffic engineering systems, LSP state is available only locally on each Label Edge Router for its own LSPs. Global LSP state can matter for some demand patterns, so a PCE that sees all of it can make better decisions. RFC 4655 had raised concerns about a stateful PCE: synchronization overhead, race conditions with out-of-band synchronization, and complex path calculation. The RFC notes that several TE algorithms nevertheless need global visibility of LSP state and ordered control of path reservations.

It also argues for a protocol rather than plain configuration tools such as a command line interface. Configuration operations are heavyweight, a configuration channel lets a malicious PCE take over the PCC, every vendor has its own information model, and state synchronization over a configuration channel can be inefficient.
sections.eli5: A planner who can only answer questions cannot see traffic jams it did not cause. If the planner is told about every route in use, it can plan much better.

sections.title: Passive and Active Stateful PCEs
sections.content:
The RFC builds on terms from RFC 8051: Stateful PCE, Passive Stateful PCE, Active Stateful PCE and Delegation. A passive stateful PCE only receives LSP State Reports so that it has an up-to-date view of the PCC's LSPs. An active stateful PCE can also update LSP attributes for LSPs that were delegated to it.

State ownership stays with the PCC. A PCC may be a Label Switching Router or a management station, and attributes received from a PCE are subject to the PCC's local policy. An active PCE decides both the values and when to make changes, but only for the small subset of parameters it controls. The operator can still set other parameters, and the PCC can talk to stateless and stateful PCEs at once, or revert an LSP to operator-defined defaults if it loses a PCE.

The new functions are capability advertisement, LSP state synchronization, LSP update request, LSP state report and LSP control delegation. Each LSP is under the control of a single PCE at any given time.
sections.eli5: A passive helper only watches and takes notes. An active helper may also be given the steering wheel for a particular trip, but the owner of the car can take it back.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
During PCEP session setup, each speaker includes the optional STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV in its OPEN object. It is TLV type 16 with length 4, and it carries 32 bits of flags of which only the U flag (LSP-UPDATE-CAPABILITY) is defined. A passive stateful speaker sets U to 0, an active stateful speaker sets it to 1.

The stateful extensions MUST NOT be used unless both speakers included the TLV. LSP delegation and LSP updates are allowed only if both set U to 1. If a speaker that supports the extensions but did not advertise the capability receives a PCUpd (at a PCC) or a PCRpt (at a PCE), it MUST send a PCErr with Error-type 19 (Invalid Operation) and SHOULD terminate the session. Even when U is not set on both sides, a PCE can still act as a passive stateful PCE and accept LSP State Reports.

PCE capabilities can also be advertised through the IGP. The RFC defines PCE-CAP-FLAGS bit 11 for active stateful PCE capability and bit 12 for passive stateful PCE capability. IGP advertisement does not replace negotiation in the PCEP session itself.
sections.eli5: Before working together, both sides say what they can do. Only if both say yes to changing routes can the helper actually change them.

sections.title: State Synchronization
sections.content:
Right after session initialization, the PCC gives the PCE a checkpoint-in-time copy of its LSP state. The PCC takes a snapshot, then sends it as a sequence of LSP State Reports in PCRpt messages, each with the SYNC flag set to 1.

The end of synchronization is a PCRpt with SYNC set to 0 for an LSP object with PLSP-ID 0. A PCC with nothing to synchronize SHOULD send only that end marker. Until synchronization is done, a PCE SHOULD NOT send PCUpd messages and a PCC SHOULD NOT send PCReq messages, so the PCE has the best possible view before it computes new paths.

The PCE does not acknowledge synchronization messages positively. If it has a problem with a report it MUST send a PCErr with Error-type 20 (LSP State Synchronization Error) and error-value 1, and terminate the session. A PCC that cannot complete synchronization MUST send Error-type 20 with error-value 5 and terminate the session. A PCE that limits the resources one PCC can use MUST send a PCNtf with Notification Type 4 and Notification Value 1 and terminate the session.
sections.eli5: When you join the planner, you first hand over a list of all the routes you are using. A special last note says the list is complete.

sections.title: Delegation, Revocation and Return
sections.content:
If both sides support LSP update, a PCC may grant a PCE a temporary right to update some attributes of an LSP. This is delegation, and it is done per LSP at any time after initialization. The PCC delegates by setting the D flag to 1 in the PCRpt, and it MUST keep D at 1 on every report for the delegation to continue. A PCE that does not accept replies at once with an empty update request with D set to 0; one that accepts sets D to 1 on its updates.

The PCC can revoke a delegation at any time by sending a report with D set to 0, ideally reverting to operator parameters in a make-before-break fashion. The PCE can return a delegation by sending a PCUpd with D set to 0. A PCE update to a non-delegated LSP draws a PCErr with Error-type 19 and error-value 1.

Two PCC-local timers handle PCE failure. The Redelegation Timeout Interval is how long the PCC waits after an unexpected session loss before revoking delegations and trying another PCE. The State Timeout Interval is how long it waits before flushing state set by the PCE and reverting to operator defaults. The State Timeout MUST be at least the Redelegation Timeout, and may be infinity. Section 9.1 suggests defaults of 30 seconds and 60 seconds respectively.

Redundant PCEs can run in hot standby: the backup receives all LSP State Reports, so no new synchronization is needed when the primary fails.
sections.eli5: Lending the steering wheel for one trip: you can take it back whenever you like, the helper can hand it back, and if the helper vanishes you wait a little and then either find another helper or go back to your own plan.

sections.title: The PCRpt and PCUpd Messages
sections.content:
Two new messages carry the stateful traffic. The PCRpt (Message-Type 10) is sent by the PCC to report the state of one or more LSPs, either asynchronously or in response to an update. Each report needs an LSP object and an intended path in an ERO, and may include the actual path in an RRO plus attribute lists. The PCUpd (Message-Type 11) is sent by the PCE and must contain an SRP object, an LSP object and an ERO in each update request. The ERO may be empty when the PCE cannot find a valid path.

An update request must contain all LSP parameters the PCE wants set, and the PCC may fill missing ones from local defaults. The PCC acts only if local policy permits. It MUST answer every processed update with a state report, reusing the SRP-ID-number. To limit traffic loss the PCC SHOULD minimize interruption and may use make-before-break from RFC 3209, in which case it reports the new path and the removal of the old path separately.

If updates arrive faster than the PCC can signal them, the PCC may compress its ingress queue by processing only the latest update for an LSP. Existing messages are also extended: PCReq and PCRep may carry the LSP object, and PCErr may carry SRP objects.
sections.eli5: One note says what state each route is in, sent by the owner. The other says what the helper wants changed, and the owner always answers what happened.

sections.title: The SRP and LSP Objects
sections.content:
The SRP object (Object-Class 33, Object-Type 1) correlates update requests with the errors and reports that answer them. Its SRP-ID-number is 32 bits, unique per session and incremented per request. The values 0x00000000 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved, and 0 is used when a report was not caused by a PCE request, such as after a link failure.

The LSP object (Object-Class 32, Object-Type 1) names the target LSP and the operation. Its PLSP-ID is 20 bits and constant for the session, and 0 and 0xFFFFF are reserved. Flags are D (delegate), S (sync), R (remove), A (administrative) and a 3-bit O operational field.

Key TLVs: LSP-IDENTIFIERS (type 18 for IPv4, type 19 for IPv6) mirror RSVP identifiers; SYMBOLIC-PATH-NAME (type 17) is a name unique in the PCC that stays constant across sessions and PCC restarts, so it is the stable identifier; LSP-ERROR-CODE (type 20) gives the failure reason; RSVP-ERROR-SPEC (type 21) carries RSVP error objects from downstream.
sections.eli5: Every request gets a ticket number so answers can be matched to questions, and every route has a short label plus a permanent nickname.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Delegation and state reporting give an adversary more information and more attack surface. The RFC RECOMMENDS using these extensions only on authenticated and encrypted sessions (TLS, per the PCEPS document) between a PCC and PCEs under the same administrative authority, following RFC 7525.

Three threats are named. LSP state snooping: eavesdroppers on unsecured sessions could learn where the network's weak points are. A PCC with several PCEs SHOULD let the operator group them by administrative domain and MUST NOT advertise an LSP to a PCE if it is delegated to a PCE in another group. Malicious PCE: it could flood the PCC with PCUpd messages; the PCC may revoke delegation at any time without justification and then drop incoming updates. Malicious PCC: the PCE keeps state per PCC, so it is RECOMMENDED to limit resources per PCC, signalled with PCNtf Notification Type 4.
sections.eli5: Telling a helper everything about your routes is risky if someone listens in or the helper goes bad. So you lock the line, and you can always take the wheel back.
